newsitem.title: GUATEMALA: U.N. chief ending term with Guatemalan peace pact.
newsitem.headline: U.N. chief ending term with Guatemalan peace pact.

text.p: Hours before ending his tenure as the world's top diplomat, Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali urged the United Nations on Sunday not to turn its back on Guatemala as it signs a major peace pact.

In a gala ceremony, government leaders and commanders of the Guatemalan National Revolutionary Movement (URNG) rebels were to sign a peace treaty on Sunday evening to end the 36-year old civil war in which 140,000 people have died or disappeared, most as a result of brutal military anti-insurgency sweeps.

Boutros-Ghali officially leaves office at midnight on Tuesday, after his hopes for a second term were derailed by the United States. He will be succeeded by Kofi Annan, a U.N. career diplomat from Ghana.

"The international community must not turn its attention away, especially in the critical early stages of implementation," he said in an apparent reference to China's objections to 155 U.N. peacekeepers needed to supervise an intricate timetable for a separation of forces, disarmament and demobilization.

Guatemala, as well as other Central American nations, has diplomatic relations and economic ties to Taiwan, which China considers a renegade province. They supported moves toward eventual U.N. membership for Taiwan, whose foreign minister, John Chang, was invited to the ceremonies.
China holds veto power in The U.N. Security Council, which continues discussions this week on approving the observers.
Boutros-Ghali recalled, in remarks prepared for delivery, that he began his five-year term with the signing of the El Salvador peace pact two weeks after he took office in 1992.
"Today, as I prepare to leave office, I am gratified to witness the signing of this agreement which constitutes a milestone for Guatemala and all of Central America," he said.
"For the first time there is peace throughout the region, with democratically elected governments in each of its countries," he added.
Boutros-Ghali said the agreement ending decades of confict should serve to heal the bitterly divided country and provide a blueprint for a democratic state.

Calling Guatemala's war a "horrible, fraticidal conflict," he said negotiators attempted to address the roots of the dispute in a series of accords dealing with "social injustice, human rights abuses, militarization of public security and discrimination against the indigenous population."

But he said the ceasefire was not an end in itself. "Rather it is a pre-condition for pursuing national reconciliation across the political, social, ethnic, cultural and linguistic divides that have stiffled Guatemala's development for many years."
The peace agreement, he said, was aimed at providing a "blueprint for strengthening the pillars of a democratic state."
"The confrontations of Central America have left hundreds of thousands of dead, many more displaced or exiled, and many survivors traumatized by their experience," he said.
"These victims should not be forgotten," he added.
The peace talks opened over five years ago, but progress was slow until the United Nations began mediating in 1994.
Sunday's visit is the third time Boutros-Ghali has gone to Guatemala. He first visited as a senior official in Egypt's foreign ministry and then as secretary-general in April 1995.
